01.r: The accusers open their case before Pilate.
01.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the middle means 'to begin', as here, with an infinitive.

02.r: Moves the scene to the charges.

05.r: Introduces the charges in their own words.

06.r: Jesus, the one they are accusing.
06.n: Literally 'this one'; the Greek puts it first, ahead of the verb. Whether it carries contempt is a judgment from the setting, not from the word; the KJV's 'this fellow' reads it that way.

07.r: They claim to have discovered him doing these things.

08.r: Leading the nation astray, the first charge.
08.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to distort, twist', and metaphorically 'to distort, pervert', citing this verse. A present participle: an ongoing activity, as they tell it.

09.r: The article with 'nation'; English uses 'our' instead.

10.n: Abbott-Smith records that in the singular the word is used of the Jewish people, and lists this verse.

11.r: The accusers claim the nation as their own.

13.r: The second charge: that he forbade the tribute.
13.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to hinder, restrain, forbid', and lists this verse among those with an accusative and an infinitive.

14.r: The tribute owed to Rome by a subject nation.
14.n: Plural in the Greek, 'tributes', the payments of tribute. Abbott-Smith defines the word as 'tribute paid by a subject nation' and cites this verse. The BSB's 'taxes' does not keep it apart from κῆνσος and τέλος, as this study does.

15.r: The emperor, to whom the tribute went.

16.r: Present infinitive: the paying of tribute as an ongoing practice.
16.n: The same verb as in the question put to Jesus about tribute, 'to give'.

18.r: The third charge: what he says of himself.

19.r: Jesus, as the subject of his own claim.

20.r: The anointed one, Israel's promised king.
20.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from χρίω and gives, among its senses as an adjective, 'anointed'; in the Septuagint it renders מָשִׁיחַ. The accusers set it beside 'a king' so that Pilate hears a political claim, a reasonable reading of why the words are paired.

21.r: The title the accusers set beside 'Christ'.

22.r: Infinitive after 'saying': the content of his claim.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus lacks ἡμῶν, 'our', and the καί before the last 'saying'. So the KJV reads 'perverting the nation' where the ASV has 'our nation', and 'saying that he himself is Christ' with no 'and'. It also has φόρους, 'tribute', in another position, which makes no difference in English.
